title: Buklod: Songs of an unfinished struggle
summary: Forty years after the EDSA Revolution, the music of folk group Buklod remains a haunting reminder of a promise left unfulfilled — and a fight that is far from over

blocks.text: Forty years after the EDSA Revolution, the music of folk group Buklod remains a haunting reminder of a promise left unfulfilled — and a fight that is far from over

items: Post-EDSA protest musicians faced challenges in a society eager to celebrate democracy, yet they continued to perform and advocate for social issues.
The folk group Buklod, consisting of Noel Cabangon, Romeo Dongeto, and Rene Boncocan, emerged from a tradition of protest artists and gained recognition for their politically charged songs.
Despite the disbandment of Buklod, their music remains relevant, resonating with current social issues and serving as a reminder of the unfinished fight for justice and equality in the Philippines.

To be an activist in the years immediately after the 1986 EDSA Revolution meant sailing against the optimistic tide that swept the nation following the ouster of the Marcos dictatorship. Democracy had been restored, Cory Aquino was president, and the mood was blazing yellow. Everyone, it seemed, wanted to move on and celebrate.

And to be a protest musician at a time when vacuous pop, delivered by singers and bands with gelled hair and shoulder pads, ruled the airwaves meant strumming an acoustic guitar in the middle of Euphoria: nobody could hear you, and those who did wished you weren’t there.

Protest musicians of the post-EDSA years did not come out of nowhere. They followed a tradition of protest artists from the ’70s and early ’80s whose songs were in the form and vernacular of folk and folk-rock: Jess Santiago, Paul Galang, Susan Fernandez, Pancho Lara, Gary Granada; folk groups like Pahayagan and Sinaglahi. Asin and Heber Bartolome’s Banyuhay carried it into the mainstream, proving that a song about the environment, or the daily struggles of working people could sell records.
The folk group Buklod was that period’s best-kept secret.

Noel Cabangon, Romeo Dongeto, and Rene Boncocan sang at political gatherings long before anyone thought of them as recording artists. Their first album, Bukid at Buhay, came out in 1988 as a trio; Boncocan left the following year, and Cabangon and Dongeto carried on as a duo in “Tatsulok” (1991) and “Sa Kandungan ng Kalikasan” (1992).

Buklod’s songs found a home in mainstream compilation albums such as Karapatang Pantao and Dear Cory, masterminded by maverick producer Ed Formoso, known for the psychedelic-folk group Dinosaur, a trio with Boy Camara and Jett Montelibano, and for birthing the supergroup Lokal Brown.
It wasn’t until “Kanlungan” was used in a burger commercial, and “Tatsulok” was covered by Bamboo many years later, that the secret was out.

“Kanlungan” became the song everyone requested from Cabangon, by then an established solo recording artist. It didn’t matter, of course, that a song about longing and the passing of time performed by activists became a jingle for an American fast food chain. Or that “Tatsulok,” an indictment of oppressive class structures, became a rock anthem for a generation largely spared from a policeman’s truncheon. By then, Buklod had long disbanded.

Buklod would jam occasionally, but there was never a full reunion or a new album. Not until 2018, 30 years after their first record, when the three went back to the studio for 3 Dekada: Ang Muling Pag-awit.

The comeback, the urge to make their voices, now older, heard again, was triggered by the brazen extra-judicial killings and rights violations under the then two-year old regime of now detained former president Rodrigo Duterte. Three decades on, the old songs still resonated and it was the trio’s way of joining the outrage.

A few nights ago, they reunited again, this time for a fund-raiser for ailing painter Federico “Boy” Dominguez, known in activist and art circles as BoyD. In the crowd were battle-hardened activists, finding comfort in familiar songs.

Forty years after EDSA, Buklod’s songs still carry the same weight as the day they were first sung. The promise of the EDSA Revolution has since soured: old and new elites, despots who use the rhetoric of democracy to undermine its values, disenchantment with its failure to lift people from chronic hunger and poverty, activists who dared to protest treated with the same iron fist as Marcos the father. And Marcos the son is back in Malacañang.

Buklod and the other post-EDSA protest artists were right all along: The revolution left too much undone. In the face of public indifference, they still said it and sang about it, even if it meant preaching to the converted, dodging bullets at rallies, raising families on a folk singer’s income, or enduring years of separation over ideological and political disagreements.

In the end, it is the songs that outlast the quarrels. Songs that bring old friends and comrades together and remind them, and the rest of us, that the fight they sang about was never finished. – Rappler.com
